section.title: One-sided limits and infinite behavior
section.p: Section gave us tools for limits that settle down to a finite number. But limits can fail, or change character, in several different ways.

A graph can approach one value from the left and another from the right. A function can grow without bound near a point. Or the input itself can move farther and farther away, so that we ask what happens at the far ends of the graph.
These are not rare exceptions. They are some of the most important behaviors calculus has to name.

subsection.title: Left-hand and right-hand limits
subsection.p: When we write x\to a, we usually mean that x approaches a from both sides. But sometimes the two sides tell different stories.

example.title: Different limits from left and right

statement.p: Consider the function
As x\to 2^- (from the left), f(x)=x+1\to 3. As x\to 2^+ (from the right), f(x)=4-x\to 2. The value f(2)=5 does not change the nearby behavior.

figure.caption: The left and right sides approach different values. Therefore the two-sided limit does not exist.

statement.p: \lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=L means that f(x) approaches L as x approaches a from values less than a (left-hand limit).
\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L means that f(x) approaches L as x approaches a from values greater than a (right-hand limit).

example.title: A removable hole has matching one-sided limits

statement.p: For g(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1} (x\neq 1), \lim_{x\to 1^-}g(x)=2 and \lim_{x\to 1^+}g(x)=2. Because both one-sided limits match, \lim_{x\to 1}g(x)=2.
For J(x)=\frac{|x|}{x} (x\neq 0), \lim_{x\to 0^-}J(x)=-1 and \lim_{x\to 0^+}J(x)=1. Since -1\neq 1, the two-sided limit does not exist.

subsection.title: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes
subsection.p: A limit can fail in a different way: values might not settle near any finite number, but grow without bound.

statement.p: Consider f(x)=\frac{1}{(x-2)^2}. As x\to 2, the denominator (x-2)^2 approaches 0 through positive numbers, so the fraction grows beyond any fixed bound.
We write \lim_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{(x-2)^2}=\infty.
We write \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\infty if f(x) can be made larger than any chosen positive number by taking x sufficiently close to a with x\neq a.
Similarly, \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=-\infty means f(x) becomes negative with arbitrarily large magnitude.

example.title: The sign determines the direction of infinity

statement.p: For g(x)=\frac{1}{x-2}, \lim_{x\to 2^-}\frac{1}{x-2}=-\infty and \lim_{x\to 2^+}\frac{1}{x-2}=\infty.

figure.caption: The graph of \frac{1}{x-2} falls without bound from the left and rises without bound from the right.

statement.p: The line x=a is a vertical asymptote of the graph of f if at least one of the one-sided limits \lim_{x\to a^-}f(x) or \lim_{x\to a^+}f(x) is \infty or -\infty.

warning.title: Hole versus asymptote
warning.p: \frac{0}{0} may hide a removable hole (when common factors cancel), whereas \frac{\text{nonzero}}{0} signals a vertical asymptote.

subsection.title: Limits at infinity
subsection.p: Many questions ask what happens after a long time or for very large input.

statement.p: Suppose coffee temperature is modeled by T(t)=70+\frac{90}{t+1} for t\ge 0. As t\to\infty, \frac{90}{t+1}\to 0, so \lim_{t\to\infty}T(t)=70.
We write \lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L if f(x) approaches L as x becomes arbitrarily large.
We write \lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=L if f(x) approaches L as x becomes negative with arbitrarily large magnitude.

If \lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L or \lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=L, then the line y=L is a horizontal asymptote of the graph of f on that end.

Consider f(x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}. For x\gt 0, f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+1/x^2}} \to 1 as x\to\infty. For x\lt 0, \sqrt{x^2+1}=|x|\sqrt{1+1/x^2}=-x\sqrt{1+1/x^2}, so f(x)=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+1/x^2}} \to -1 as x\to-\infty.
This graph has two horizontal asymptotes: y=1 as x\to\infty and y=-1 as x\to-\infty.

For f(x)=\frac{x^2+1}{x-1}, polynomial division gives \frac{x^2+1}{x-1}=x+1+\frac{2}{x-1}. As x\to\infty, \frac{2}{x-1}\to 0, so y=x+1 is a slant asymptote.

subsection.p: These ideas help us describe graphs accurately. But the word approaches is still informal. The next section turns it into a test that does not depend on the drawing or the table: make the output error smaller than any tolerance named.
